title: Natural Language Processing Fundamentals
learning_outcomes: Explain natural Language Processing Fundamentals and connect at least two of its listed subtopics.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will study natural Language Processing Fundamentals within Specialized Fields of Artificial Intelligence. You will connect the syllabus topics below to a small, inspectable example and practice stating what the evidence does—and does not—support.

content_blocks.title: The central idea
content_blocks.text: Natural language processing represents text as data for tasks such as classification, extraction, search, or generation. Tokenization and normalization choices affect downstream meaning and should fit the language and task.

content_blocks.title: Syllabus topics covered in this lesson

items.title: Language as structured data
items.text: Language as structured data is one of the concepts used to reason about natural language processing fundamentals. Define the inputs, assumptions, and intended result in this context, then test the idea on a small representative example and document where it may not apply.

items.title: Text normalization
items.text: Scaling transforms numeric features to a common range or statistical scale. Fit scaling parameters on training data only and apply the same learned transformation to validation, test, and production inputs.

items.title: Tokenization
items.text: Tokenization turns text into units that a model or text pipeline can process. Tokens need not match words, and the tokenizer affects sequence length, vocabulary coverage, and cost.

items.title: Stemming and lemmatization
items.text: Stemming and lemmatization is one of the concepts used to reason about natural language processing fundamentals. Define the inputs, assumptions, and intended result in this context, then test the idea on a small representative example and document where it may not apply.

items.title: Stop words and vocabulary
items.text: Stop words and vocabulary is one of the concepts used to reason about natural language processing fundamentals. Define the inputs, assumptions, and intended result in this context, then test the idea on a small representative example and document where it may not apply.

items.title: Bag-of-words and TF-IDF
items.text: TF–IDF weights a term using its frequency in a document and its rarity across a collection. It is a useful sparse baseline but does not represent semantic similarity as a contextual embedding does.

items.title: Text classification applications
items.text: Text classification applications is one of the concepts used to reason about natural language processing fundamentals. Define the inputs, assumptions, and intended result in this context, then test the idea on a small representative example and document where it may not apply.

content_blocks.title: Common mistakes and fixes
content_blocks.text: If the output differs, check indentation and spelling, confirm you saved the intended file, and compare each input value with the example. If the example runs as expected, do not infer that it proves a trained model works; this snippet is a deterministic teaching aid. Keep sensitive data out of tests.

content_blocks.title: Check before you trust a result
content_blocks.text: This is a small, deterministic teaching example—not a trained AI model or evidence of production performance. Run it with a local Python 3 interpreter; do not paste secrets or private data into experiments.

task_acceptance_criteria: Explain the core concept and accurately refer to the source syllabus topics.
Record a prediction and compare it with a reproducible result or a clearly stated manual trace.
Document at least one limitation, safety consideration, or evaluation requirement.
hints: Write down the inputs, expected output, and assumptions before changing the example.
Change only one input or condition and compare the results with your original prediction.
Ask whether the example covers realistic cases, important subgroups, and failure conditions; a toy example does not establish production reliability.
troubleshooting: Use Python 3 and run the file from the folder where it was saved.
If output differs, restore the original input and compare one changed value at a time.
If Python reports a syntax error, check copied quotation marks, indentation, and whether the full code block was copied.
These examples require no external packages, network access, model credentials, or personal data.
